newsitem.title: USA: FCC chief rejects idea of commercials on public TV.
newsitem.headline: FCC chief rejects idea of commercials on public TV.

text.p: The nation's top communications regulator Monday urged public television stations to reject the idea of accepting paid commercials to shore up their finances and bankroll quality programming.

"While I honour those who are searching for creative ways to keep public TV strong, the recent proposal to run commercials on PBS two nights a week would, in my opinion, fundamentally alter the non-commercial nature of this unique and vital broadcasting service," Federal Communications Commission Chairman Reed Hundt said.
"It reminds me of those non-alcoholic beers Sharps and O'Doul's -- it's delusional," he added in a speech to a conference sponsored by the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg Public Policy Centre.
The former president of the PBS network, Lawrence Grossman, has proposed allowing commercials two nights a week on otherwise commercial-free public TV.

At least half a dozen big public TV stations -- including those in Chicago, Philadelphia, Detroit, St. Louis, Minneapolis-St. Paul and Miami -- are reported to be considering the idea. But other big stations oppose the plan.
A handful of stations in the early 1980's experimented temporarily with paid ads.
Currently, corporations that underwrite public-TV programmes are allowed to run on-air announcements about their companies. But the underwriters do not peddle particular products.
Hundt, meanwhile, urged Congress to supply public TV with enough money -- "hundreds of millions of dollars" -- to keep the system adequately financed over the long term.
